extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, advocates, and practitioners who need to understand or respond to federal notices of proposed rulemaking (NPRMs)
extracted.subtask_description: Explains what a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) is and the key information it must include under the Administrative Procedure Act and related guidance (e.g., type of rule, comment timing, how to file). Useful for people drafting, reviewing, or preparing comments on NPRMs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication in the Federal Register
rubrics_metrics.description: A notice of proposed rulemaking is a notice in the Federal Register that announces the intent of an agency to promulgate a particular rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication of an NPRM is often the first time the public becomes aware of an agency's proposed rule; agencies post NPRMs in the Federal Register to announce the proposed action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required information in the NPRM (Administrative Procedure Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires agencies to specify certain information in the NPRM, such as the type of rule involved, the timing of public comments, and how the comments are to be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing or evaluating an NPRM, check that it identifies the rule type, provides clear deadlines and procedures for submitting comments, and includes any other statutorily required content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: When posting an NPRM, an agency will also announce an opportunity for public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies typically provide a period during which stakeholders can submit feedback; the NPRM should clearly describe how and where to submit comments and what the comment process entails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended comment period length (E.O. 12866 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: E.O. 12866 states that most rulemakings should include a comment period of 60 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most agencies provide a 60-day or longer comment period for complex or controversial rules; consider whether additional time is warranted for particularly technical or far-reaching proposals.
